tip: The -an ending makes a who-does form: ‘karate yapan sporcu’ means the athlete who does karate, with no separate who word.
The -alım ending makes a we-suggestion: ‘buluşalım’ = let's meet. Adding ‘mı’ turns it into a question, so ‘buluşalım mı’ asks shall we.
‘okuduğum’ means that I read: the -dığım ending on a verb builds a describing phrase, so ‘okuduğum kitap’ = the book that I read.
The -erek ending means by doing something: ‘dinleyerek’ = by listening, telling you how the falling asleep happens.
‘geldiği için’ means because it came: a verb plus -dığı için gives the reason, here why I missed the meeting.
‘kalkıp’ uses -ıp to chain verbs under one tense: ‘geç kalkıp kahvaltı hazırlarız’ = we wake up late and make breakfast.
‘konuştukça’ uses -dıkça for the more, the more: ‘konuştukça anlıyorum’ = the more I talk, the more I understand.
‘gitmek yerine’ means instead of going: the -mek verb form plus ‘yerine’ expresses choosing one action over another.
‘dağıtılır’ is a no-doer form: the -ıl ending drops the doer, so it means letters are distributed with no mention of who does it.
‘oynardık’ means we used to play: the -rdık ending marks a repeated past habit, not a single event.
‘ne yaparsam yapayım’ means whatever I do: the frame repeats the verb, ‘yaparsam’ then ‘yapayım’, to say no matter what.
‘her gidişimde’ means every time I go: ‘her’ (each) plus the action noun ‘gidiş’ with -imde marks each occasion something happens.
Turkish adds an apostrophe before a suffix on a proper name: ‘Fatma'nın’ = Fatma's, keeping the name readable.
‘her ne kadar’ with a later ‘da’ means although: ‘her ne kadar yorgun olsam da’ = no matter how tired I am.
The -ince ending means when or as soon as: ‘gelince’ = when it comes, so ‘sonbahar gelince’ is when autumn arrives.
The -arak ending means by doing something: ‘oynayarak’ = by playing, showing how they spent the time.
‘vermeseydi’ (if he had not made it) sets up an unreal past, and ‘olurdu’ (would be) gives the imagined result.
‘her ne kadar’ opens an although idea closed by -sa da: ‘olsam da’ = even though I am, so it reads although I am tired.
‘varmış olmalılar’ joins past -mış with ‘olmalı’ (must) to infer about the past: they must have arrived by now.
‘diye’ after a verb marks purpose: ‘değmesin diye’ = so that it does not touch, here to keep the evil eye away.
The -urduk ending marks a past habit: ‘otururduk’ = we used to sit, a repeated past routine, not one single sitting.
‘gelince’ means when it comes. The -ince ending marks the moment one action triggers another, so no separate word for when is needed.
‘kazanmış’ uses the -mış past for things you did not witness yourself, giving a sense of apparently or so I heard rather than a plain fact.
‘gördüğüm’ means that I saw and describes ‘manzara’ (view). The -dığım ending turns a verb into a describing phrase for the noun after it.
‘olduktan sonra’ means after becoming. The -dıktan sonra pattern on a verb marks doing the main action after that one finishes.
‘gelene kadar’ means until you come. The -ene kadar ending sets a deadline that the main action reaches or finishes by.
‘danışsaydın’ is the if you had consulted form. The -saydın ending marks a past condition that did not actually happen.
-li turns a place into from there: ‘nere’ plus -li plus -siniz gives ‘nerelisiniz’, where are you from.
‘yaşındayım’ = I am ... years old: ‘yaş’ (age) + -ında + -yım. Turkish states age with this being ending, no verb for to be.
The yes/no word harmonizes with the last vowel: after ‘boş’ (o) it becomes ‘mu’, so ‘bu yer boş mu’ asks is this seat free.
